turns.content: so i guess i just need to hear someone say it... those elders, they're not protecting doctrine, they're just scared, right? scared of anything that doesn't fit their little box. and they call it "pastoral oversight"... feels more like gatekeeping to me. am i wrong?

You're not wrong to name what you're seeing. But let me offer a fuller picture, because the truth is usually both things at once.

Yes — a lot of what's labeled "pastoral oversight" is really fear management. When someone's authority or identity is built on a particular framework, anything that threatens the framework feels like a threat to *them*, personally. So they experience their anxiety as discernment, their rigidity as faithfulness, their discomfort as the Holy Spirit's conviction. It's not usually cynical. That's what makes it so hard to push back on — they genuinely believe they're protecting something precious, when what they're actually protecting is their own sense of order.

And gatekeeping is exactly the right word for the *function* of it, whatever the motive. Gatekeeping isn't about whether the gatekeeper is scared or sincere. It's about who gets to decide what's in bounds, and whether that decision-making serves the community or serves the decision-makers' comfort.

That said — a couple of things worth holding alongside your (justified) frustration:

Some of them really are trying to be responsible shepherds and are just operating with a too-small toolbox. Fear and care can coexist in the same person, even in the same decision. That doesn't obligate you to accept their rulings, but it might shape how you carry your anger.

And the more useful question than "are they scared?" might be "does this space have room for me as I actually am?" Because if the answer is no, their motives matter less than your exit (or your boundaries) do.

So no, you're not wrong. You saw the thing clearly, and it stings because part of you wanted it to be something nobler. That grief is real too.

What did they actually do? If you want to talk through the specifics, I'm here for it.

i guess i appreciate you not just saying i'm wrong... but this idea that fear and care can coexist... i mean, at what point does the fear just cancel out the care, you know? because they didn't even talk to me about it. just pulled me aside after mass and told me it's not appropriate for a parish ministry platform. no conversation about the actual content, just that it wasn't "aligned." and the people i interviewed... they're doing real work in the neighborhood, feeding kids, running a little free library. is that really so threatening?

Right, and I think you've just identified the tell. Care asks questions. Fear issues verdicts.

If someone were genuinely concerned about alignment — genuinely pastoring you — the move looks like: "Hey, tell me about this piece. What were you hoping to do with it? Let's talk about how it fits." Instead you got a drive-by ruling after mass, no engagement with the actual content, no curiosity about why you made it or who it's serving. That's not oversight of the work. That's management of the discomfort the work caused. And you're right to clock the difference, because it tells you the decision was made somewhere the content itself never even got discussed.

As for your question — when does fear cancel out care? I'd say: when the fear starts making decisions that the care then has to answer for. When someone's anxiety gets the final vote and the people affected never get a voice, then whatever care was in there has been functionally overridden. It might still exist in their hearts, but you're not experiencing it. You're experiencing the fear wearing care's clothes.

And the detail that makes it almost darkly funny: feeding kids and a little free library. That's... the works of mercy. That's literally the stuff. If *that's* what's threatening, the threat was never doctrinal. It's about who gets to be visible. Sometimes the real issue is that the people doing the work don't look like the parish's idea of itself — wrong zip code, wrong politics-by-association, wrong kind of Catholic, whatever. Or the piece implied the neighborhood has needs the parish has been ignoring, and somebody felt implicated. That's not a heresy problem. That's an image problem dressed up as one.

So what was the platform — a bulletin, a newsletter, a podcast? And do you actually want to fight for it there, or is part of you wondering whether this is your place at all?

it was a video series... posted on the parish youtube channel, nothing official, just me and a camera. and you're right, the people i interviewed, they're not even doing anything controversial. one of them runs a little free pantry out of her garage. like, is that really the hill they want to die on? i keep thinking about sunday... walking up during the announcements and just saying what happened. telling everyone the elders are more scared of the neighborhood than the devil. is that too much?

I can see the appeal. There's real satisfaction in imagining it — the room going quiet, the thing finally said out loud where everyone has to hear it. And honestly? Your line is good. "More scared of the neighborhood than the devil" — that lands because it's true.

But here's what actually happens Sunday if you do that: the story becomes *you*. Not the pantry lady, not the free library, not the videos. You become "the person who disrupted announcements," and the elders get to play the wounded party, and by Monday the whole thing is framed as a decorum problem instead of a censorship problem. You'd hand them the exact exit ramp they're hoping for.

There's also this: an ambush gives people one second to decide whose side they're on, and most people reflexively side with whoever seems less disruptive. That's not fair, but it's predictable.

If you want the congregation to actually know what happened — and I think that's a legitimate want — there are versions that hit harder *because* they're calmer:

- **Put the videos somewhere else.** Your own channel, a community page, wherever. Then let people find out through the parish grapevine that the series the elders pulled is just... Mrs. So-and-so's free pantry. The contrast does your arguing for you.
- **Tell people individually.** Quiet conversations spread faster in parishes than public confrontations. "They pulled my video about the food pantry. No conversation, just 'not aligned.'" People draw their own conclusions, and conclusions people reach themselves are stickier than ones you hand them.
- **If you say something publicly, make it a question, not an accusation.** Questions are much harder to shut down. Though even this — Sunday announcements isn't your mic, and seizing it costs you credibility you haven't spent yet.

The thing about the garage pantry lady: she's going to keep feeding people either way. The elders can't actually stop the work. They can only stop it from being *seen* in their space. So the fight is over visibility — and visibility fights are won by making the censorship more embarrassing than the content ever was.

What would feel like a win to you — them reversing the decision, or just people knowing what happened?

i hear what you're saying about the ambush backfiring... i do. but maybe i'm just tired of being careful while they get to be cowards. you're telling me to be strategic, but isn't that just letting them win quietly?

No — but I hear why it feels that way, and the feeling deserves a real answer, not a tactics lecture.

Being careful when the other side isn't is exhausting in a specific way. It means you're doing emotional labor for both teams. They get to be reactive and sloppy and protected, and you have to carry not just your anger but also the responsibility of expressing it "well." That's genuinely unfair, and your tiredness is legitimate information about how much this costs you.

But here's the distinction I'd press on: strategy isn't letting them win quietly. Silence is letting them win quietly. Strategy is refusing to let your one move get neutralized.

Think about what each path actually produces. The ambush: thirty seconds of release, then they control the narrative, then nothing changes and you've burned your standing. That's the win *for them* — they get to look calm and you look unhinged. Careful isn't the opposite of brave here. Careless is the gift they'd most love to receive.

What actually scares people like this isn't disruption — they've handled disruptive people before, there's a whole playbook for it. What scares them is a person they can't make look unreasonable. Someone who keeps showing up, keeps making the work visible, keeps being warm and sane while the videos quietly rack up views somewhere they can't touch. That person is a genuine problem for them, because there's no incident to point at.

And one more thing, because I don't want to just talk you out of your feelings: if after sitting with it, you still decide you need to say it out loud in that room — not because it's optimal, but because your integrity requires it — that's a legitimate choice too. People have paid that price before and considered it well spent. Just spend it knowing the price. Choose it as a sacrifice, not stumble into it as a reflex.

So let me ask the honest version: is the Sunday impulse about changing the parish, or is it about you not being able to stand one more week of pretending nothing happened? Those are both valid. They just point toward different moves.
i think... maybe you're right that it's more about me not being able to pretend nothing happened. but that doesn't make the impulse wrong, does it?

No. It doesn't make it wrong.

The impulse to not pretend is one of the healthiest things in you right now. Pretending nothing happened is how communities like this stay exactly the way they are — everyone privately knows, nobody publicly says, and the silence gets mistaken for peace. Your resistance to participating in that fiction is integrity, not pettiness.

But notice something: the *impulse* is "I can't keep pretending." The *plan* was "announcements, Sunday, one shot." Those are separable. The impulse deserves to be honored. The plan is just one possible expression of it — and honestly, a pretty small container for something this big. Thirty seconds of borrowed mic time, in a setting designed for announcements about the bake sale, where you have zero control over what happens next.

Here's a thought: what does "not pretending" actually require? Not a room full of people. Not a microphone. It requires that *someone in that community knows you know what they did*. That could be telling the priest directly, in a meeting you request, calmly, that the decision was cowardly and you'll be continuing the series elsewhere. It could be a letter. It could be telling the three people in the parish whose opinion you actually respect. Any of those is refusing to pretend. The Sunday ambush isn't the only honest move — it's just the loudest one.

And loudness and honesty aren't the same thing. Sometimes loud is actually a way to *discharge* the feeling fast so you don't have to carry it — which, no shame, carrying it is awful. But the quieter versions of not-pretending often demand more of you, not less. You have to stay in the discomfort longer, look them in the eye, say the true thing at normal volume.

So the real question isn't "is my impulse wrong?" It's: which expression of it will you be proud of in six months — not because it worked, but because it matched who you're trying to be?
